entries.text: Build a production-ready local file-transfer application that makes transferring files between two laptops on the same Wi-Fi/LAN extremely fast, reliable, secure, and effortless.
* Pair two laptops in seconds with minimal user interaction.
* Support single files, multiple files, folders, and very large files.
* Transfer directly over the local network at the highest practical Wi-Fi/LAN speed.
* Keep memory usage bounded even for 10 GB, 50 GB, 100 GB+ transfers.
* Resume interrupted transfers instead of restarting them.
* Recover cleanly from Wi-Fi drops, refreshes, sleep/wake, crashes, and reconnects.
* Verify transferred data using cryptographic hashes so corrupted files can never be reported as successfully transferred.
* Make pairing secure enough that files cannot accidentally be sent to the wrong device.
* Hide WebRTC, ports, networking, SDP, OPFS, and other technical concepts from normal users.
* Provide a simple UX: **Send → Select Files → Pair → Transfer → Verified Complete**.
* Show accurate transfer speed, progress, ETA, transferred size, and connection status.
* Require no internet or cloud storage for local transfers.
* Avoid forcing users to reselect or rehash huge files when only the connection fails.
* Handle thousands of files and multi-gigabyte transfers without freezes, crashes, corrupted state, or excessive disk/network overhead.
* Provide clear recovery actions whenever something goes wrong.

**A non-technical user should be able to open the app on two laptops, connect them in seconds, transfer a huge file at near the maximum speed their Wi-Fi and disks allow, recover automatically from temporary failures, and receive a cryptographically verified copy without needing to understand how the application works.**
The application must prioritize, in order:
**Correctness → Data integrity → Reliability → Pairing simplicity → Transfer speed → Security → UX → Visual polish.**
You are the principal engineer, security reviewer, performance engineer, QA lead, UX engineer, and release owner for this application.
The application is scheduled for production release in **2 days**.
Your job is NOT to merely audit it.
**audit → reproduce → fix → refactor where necessary → add tests → benchmark → retest → attempt to break it again → fix remaining issues → produce release evidence.**
Treat every bug you leave behind as a production incident.
Do not stop because existing tests pass.
Do not assume code is correct because it looks sophisticated.
Do not preserve an implementation merely because it already exists.
At the same time, do not perform pointless rewrites. Preserve the existing architecture where it is sound and make targeted, production-quality changes.
This should become an extremely simple and dependable way to transfer files between **two laptops connected to the same local Wi-Fi/LAN/hotspot**.
The primary experience should feel approximately like:
6. Verify the intended device with minimal friction.
8. See real speed, ETA, progress and status.
9. Transfer completes and is cryptographically verified.
5. Choose destination at the appropriate point.
7. Interrupted transfers resume instead of restarting.
9. User gets an unmistakable success state.
The user should NOT have to understand:
The product must hide complexity unless something goes wrong, in which case diagnostics must clearly explain what the user can do.
Study the entire repository before changing anything.
Current design includes several good ideas that should not be casually destroyed:
Preserve those properties unless you can replace them with something demonstrably better.

Where real two-runtime LAN behavior cannot run in CI, create a separate integration harness and clearly document the manual release test.
Build a deterministic test harness capable of injecting:
The objective is not simply “error displayed”.
**no silent corruption, no incorrect success, and a clear path to recovery.**
Do NOT hardcode fake target numbers if the underlying device cannot reach them.
On localhost / same-machine synthetic tests, protocol implementation overhead should not be the dominant bottleneck.
On a modern LAN, transfer should be primarily constrained by:
not by thousands of synchronous 60-KiB durability flushes or excessive JSON control traffic.
A performance regression greater than 10% requires explanation.
* whole source isn't loaded into RAM;
* whole destination isn't loaded into RAM;
Keep memory approximately bounded independent of total transfer size.
* one command that executes the complete release gate
* no console errors during normal flow
At minimum CI must perform a clean:
followed by the complete check command.
Before declaring release-ready, define and execute/document this matrix:
Windows laptop A → Windows laptop B.
For each test verify the final SHA/file tree.
Give the application to someone who knows nothing about its implementation.
They should be able to send a file between two laptops without reading the README.
If they need to understand ports, OPFS, Node, SDP, ICE or WebRTC, the UX has failed.
Do not hide problems with giant try/catch blocks.
Do not convert corruption into success.
Do not disable verification for speed.
Do not solve crashes by loading everything into memory.
Do not delete partially received valid data unnecessarily.
Do not restart a 100 GB transfer because pairing failed.
Do not make the user repeat expensive hashing without a security/integrity reason.
Do not claim a device is verified unless it actually is.
Do not display “100% complete” before authoritative verification succeeds.
Do not call something “saved” until destination verification succeeds.
Do not require internet access for transfer.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, trackers or external services.
